questions.q: What is the four-part structure every project write-up in this lab uses?
options: Introduction, Background, Methodology, Conclusion
Claim, Method, Result, Limitation
Problem, Solution, Benchmark, Future Work
Hypothesis, Experiment, Data, Discussion
questions.explain: Every project write-up in this lab, including Project 3's, uses the same claim/method/result/limitation structure.

questions.q: Which of these would be an overreaching claim this write-up explicitly avoids making?
options: The agent always beats SQL Server's optimizer
The agent still loses on some boundary-case episodes
The agent matched or beat the optimizer's default plan on 78% of held-out episodes
The average logical-read reduction on wins was 34%
questions.explain: The claim deliberately avoids overstating the result — 22% of held-out episodes the agent ties or loses, so 'always beats' would misrepresent the finding.

questions.q: What numbers does the Result section report from Lesson 8?
options: Only the training loss curve from Lesson 7
Only the 78% win-or-tie rate, since that's the headline number
The 78% win-or-tie rate against the optimizer's default plan, and the 34% average logical-read reduction on episodes won
The number of SQL tables joined in the query
questions.explain: A complete result section reports both the win rate and the magnitude of improvement on wins, not just one flattering number.

questions.q: Why does the Limitation section explicitly name the boundary-case regression rather than omitting it?
options: Because the boundary-case regression actually improves the win rate
Because a project write-up that only reports the win rate and hides where the agent still loses isn't a complete, trustworthy result
Because Lesson 8 did not actually find this failure mode
Because omitting it would violate stable-baselines3's license
questions.explain: The lesson frames naming real limitations plainly as central to what makes a write-up trustworthy, rather than marketing.

questions.q: What is one limitation this write-up names about the RL framing itself, beyond the boundary-case regression?
options: That AdventureWorks2012 does not contain a Customer table
That the agent never learned to pick FORCE ORDER at all
That each episode is a single decision — a contextual bandit — framed as RL for consistency with the rest of the lab, not because it's genuinely sequential
That PPO cannot be implemented in stable-baselines3
questions.explain: The write-up notes that the single-step episode structure means the result doesn't demonstrate anything about genuinely sequential, delayed-reward RL problems.
